terminal.description: A shell that starts in the shop's top folder. Move with cd, and run pwd whenever you are not sure where you are.

tasks.title: Go deep and say where you are
tasks.description:
Hesper wants the notes from last autumn's market stall, which are somewhere in `archive`. Move the shell into `archive/2025/autumn`, run `pwd` there, and write the line it prints after `inside:` in `notes.txt`.

Check compares your line with the full path of `archive/2025/autumn` in this workspace.
nextSteps: Run `ls archive` to see which folders it holds, then go one level deeper.
Move into `archive/2025/autumn`, in one step or in three.
Run `pwd` there and copy the line it prints.
hints: The lesson's command for changing the working folder is two letters long.
`cd` takes a path, and a path can name several folders joined by `/`.
Run `cd archive/2025/autumn`, then `pwd`, and copy that line after `inside:`.

tasks.title: Point from orders to the March invoices
tasks.description:
Idris works with the shell inside `orders` and wants to list the March invoices without leaving it. Write a relative path that leads from `orders` to `invoices/march` after `back:` in `notes.txt`. It must not start with `/` or `~`.

Try it first: go into `orders` and run `ls` with your path. When it lists the March invoices, write it down.

Check follows your path from `orders` and sees where it ends.
nextSteps: Work out where `invoices` sits compared with `orders`.
Build a path that first climbs out of `orders`, then goes down to `march`.
Test it with `ls` from inside `orders`, then write it after `back:`.
hints: From inside `orders`, the name `invoices` alone finds nothing: `invoices` is not inside `orders`.
`..` is the folder above. Both `orders` and `invoices` sit in the same folder above you.
The path starts with `../`, then names `invoices`, then `march`, joined with `/`.

tasks.title: Write the cd that reaches client proofs
tasks.description:
The proofs for clients sit in a folder whose name has a space in it: `client proofs`. From the top folder, move into it with `cd`. When it works, write the whole command you typed after `proofs:` in `notes.txt`, starting with `cd`.

Check runs your command from the top folder and sees where it ends.
nextSteps: Go back to the top folder, the one the terminal started in.
Try `cd` with the folder's name and read what the shell says.
Change the command so the shell reads the name as one name.
When `pwd` shows you are in `client proofs`, write the command after `proofs:`.
hints: A space separates the parts of a command. The lesson shows two ways to keep a space inside one name.
Put the whole name in quotes, or put a backslash in front of the space. Tab can also write the name for you.
The command is `cd` followed by `"client proofs"`, with the quotes.
